question:
Using only the paths and the directions shown, how many different routes are there from \(M\) to \(N?\)

[Figure 1](figures/1986_AMC_8_Q09_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
Every route must start by going from \(M\) to either \(A\) or \(B\). Separating these two possibilities helps us avoid counting a route twice.

After reaching \(A\), we can go directly to \(C\), or go through \(D\) to \(C\). From \(C\), the only next destination is \(N\). This gives two routes:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&M\to A\to C\to N,\\
&M\to A\to D\to C\to N.
\end{aligned}
\]
After reaching \(B\), we can go to \(N\), to \(C\), or to \(A\). The last possibility has the two continuations just described. Thus there are four routes starting with \(MB\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
&M\to B\to N,\\
&M\to B\to C\to N,\\
&M\to B\to A\to C\to N,\\
&M\to B\to A\to D\to C\to N.
\end{aligned}
\]
These lists include every allowed choice at each junction, and their sequences of paths are all different. Therefore there are \(2+4=\boxed{6}\) routes, choice \(\text{E}\).

edges.reason: Outcome enumeration provides concrete practice partitioning and counting finite outcomes. Probability ratios are unnecessary, as Gemini notes, but that does not erase the useful enumeration component.
Systematic pair listing practices completeness and avoiding double counts. Its multiplication structure is not needed to add disjoint category sizes, so keep the broad counting preparation only.
edges.scope: systematic counting without repetition or omission

edges.reason: Addition within ten includes the sums within five. Only the overlapping addition facts are necessary, not a prior course-completion claim.
Interpreting sums with values six through ten requires those number and quantity meanings.

Both external rejections assume every category is small, but the source states no count bound. Two-digit comparison is useful for legitimate larger collections; pairing objects or comparing smaller counts avoids that specific procedure, so retain preparation without inventing either a mandatory or an excluded range.
edges.scope: Comparing recorded category counts when the chosen collections have two-digit totals

edges.reason: The target chooses and states a sorting criterion before counting classes, directly containing classification-by-one-standard meaning.
